Messages.Author: Jan-Christophe Hoogendoorn
Messages.Body:
Hello.

I have a question about "shadow of the beast" (SOTB).

My vampire has inferior protean.
I play SOTB, so he gets an optional maneuvre each combat.
Next turn, I play a protean discipline card on my vampire.
Does he get the optional press ?

I'm sorry if this question has been asked before, but I couldn't find the
answer on the WW web-page.

Jan-Christophe Hoogendoorn.

Messages.Author: Michelle Strinja
Messages.Body:
you must get the superior when you become superior just like a raven spy
gains an extra life when animalism disipline card is played on its owner

Messages.Author: James Moe
Messages.Body:
That is actually incorrect.

From the section in the errata about minion cards...

"A discipline-based card that is put into play is put into play at either
basic or superior level. Once in play, you can't change which level it was
played at, even if you give the vampre that played it a better ability."

So, in answer to the original poster's question, no. If the card is played
at basic level, it stays at basic level.

news:3930C972...@sk.sympatico.ca...

Messages.Author: X_Ze...@email.msn.com
Messages.Body:
> > "A discipline-based card that is put into play is put into play at
> > either basic or superior level. Once in play, you can't change
> > which level it was played at, even if you give the vampre that
> > played it a better ability."
> >
> > So, in answer to the original poster's question, no. If the card
> > is played at basic level, it stays at basic level.
>
> Correct. Likewise, a Raven Spy would not receive an extra life
> when his employer gains superior animalism (nor would he lose a
> life if his employer *lost* superior animalism).

Here is where I think that the errata goes contrary to the spirit of the
game. V.TES is a game that should be able to be played without taking
notes. I only say this because I know in some tournaments I have played
in it wasn't that the issue was brought up but rather that it wasn't
(which seems rather confusing so stick with me here).

A good example of this is at a four player table on round 1 a player
bring out a size 4 Nosferatu with basic animalism. On turn two he
retains a raven spy with one life. On turn 3 he plays a animalism skill
card his Nosferatu therefore making his discipline superior. The problem
doesn't arise here but rather 7 turns later when someone tries to shoot
the raven spy with a zip gun (or a saturday night special, or aid from
bats). Now everyone including the player who controls the nosferatu
tries to remember whether the raven spy was before the skill card or
after. Often most players will get the benifit of the doubt that the
nosferatu had superior animalism.

Now this is how I have seen it play in tournaments. I think the errata
was well intentioned, but misguided because it makes the game far more
tedious to remember which went where and when. I know this may seem
like a corner case but that is why the errata was writen, and that
permanent plus one intercept has serious effect on table balance.

Comments Welcome,
Norman S. Brown Jr.
X_Zealot
Archon of the Swamp

In response to both you and tim, the reason most people are a little
wary of people putting counters on their retainers is that they tend to
float from the retainer to the vampire that retained it. Inadvertently
giving them extra blood which can make a difference between a torpored
vamp and a non-torpored vamp. Although two different colored counters
seem like a good idea, I have not seen it in effect in a game.

Messages.Body:

Well, I had that problem. Then I bought some more smaller counters. And
now I use white, bigger counters as pool and blood on the Vampires, and
smaller, blue counters for retainers, allies and mastercards. That way
now problems can occur, poolwise. I have also seen people use dice
instead of life counters on retainers. But honestly, I would contantly
be taking notes at any tournament concerning these type of things, as
long as the rules state I can.

Messages.Body:
X_Ze...@email.msn.com wrote:
>
> > > "A discipline-based card that is put into play is put into play at
> > > either basic or superior level. Once in play, you can't change
> > > which level it was played at, even if you give the vampre that
> > > played it a better ability."
> > >

> > > is played at basic level, it stays at basic level.
> >
> > Correct. Likewise, a Raven Spy would not receive an extra life
> > when his employer gains superior animalism (nor would he lose a
> > life if his employer *lost* superior animalism).
>
> Here is where I think that the errata goes contrary to the spirit of the
> game.

It is not errata. Errata would be required to have the card *change*
after being put into play when nothing on card text says to change it.

> V.TES is a game that should be able to be played without taking
> notes. I only say this because I know in some tournaments I have played
> in it wasn't that the issue was brought up but rather that it wasn't
> (which seems rather confusing so stick with me here).

No notes are required for the Raven case: just look at the retainer. If it
has two life on it, then it was put into play at superior. If it has
one, then it was probably put into play at inferior (although it could
have been superior and victimized by a Cryptic Mission - which has the
same result).

How do you remember the level at which Seeds of Corruption or Disarm was
played? A certain amount of history is implied in the texts of certain
cards. If that history poses a problem, then notes should be taken.
Errata'ing the ones that happen to stay on the vampire that played them
won't solve all of the "problems".

> A good example of this is at a four player table on round 1 a player
> bring out a size 4 Nosferatu with basic animalism. On turn two he
> retains a raven spy with one life. On turn 3 he plays a animalism skill
> card his Nosferatu therefore making his discipline superior. The problem
> doesn't arise here but rather 7 turns later when someone tries to shoot
> the raven spy with a zip gun (or a saturday night special, or aid from
> bats). Now everyone including the player who controls the nosferatu
> tries to remember whether the raven spy was before the skill card or
> after. Often most players will get the benifit of the doubt that the
> nosferatu had superior animalism.

Since the Raven has only one life on him at the time (which he loses
when he gets shot), it doesn't matter at what level he was played -
he's still out of life, and so he burns.

> Now this is how I have seen it play in tournaments. I think the errata
> was well intentioned, but misguided because it makes the game far more
> tedious to remember which went where and when. I know this may seem
> like a corner case but that is why the errata was writen, and that
> permanent plus one intercept has serious effect on table balance.

It isn't errata.

is burned" [6.1.4]

> Nice, and it would have won me a sealed-deck game two

shot
> dead by a deer rifle]!

> Different colours to the blood/pool counters, presumably.

Not typically - we just put the blood counters representing life on
the retainer card and the blood counters representing blood on the
vampire. (And we even use the same blood counters to represent a
players pool.)

> > How do you remember the level at which Seeds of Corruption or
> > Disarm was played? A certain amount of history is implied in

> > then notes should be taken.
